strengths: Addresses a genuine and practically important problem: non-differentiable rewards in biomolecular design that cannot be handled by gradient-based methods

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple domains (protein, DNA, small molecules) with consistent improvements over strong baselines (DDPO, DDPP, SFT) and competitive performance vs. DRAKES
Clear and well-motivated algorithmic framework with three intuitive phases: off-policy roll-in for exploration, value-guided roll-out for weighting, and forward KL distillation for stability
Theoretical insight connecting PPO objectives to reverse KL divergence (Theorem 1) with clear motivation for why forward KL may improve stability and reduce mode collapse

Excellent reproducibility practices: detailed hyperparameters, promised code release, comprehensive appendices, and good ablation studies on key design choices (lazy update interval K, roll-in mixture β)
Strong empirical improvements: meaningful gains on binding affinity (pLDDT 0.82 vs 0.55), DNA activity (8.28 vs 7.38), and molecular docking (9.4 vs 8.5)
Well-presented with clear figures, good motivation, and helpful visualizations of generated biomolecules with quantitative quality assessments
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: soft-optimal policies are standard in entropy-regularized MDPs, and value-weighted MLE is from prior RL work (Peters et al., 2010); the contribution is primarily a sensible combination of known techniques rather than a fundamental advance

Critical approximation (soft value function as point estimate v̂_{t-1} := r(x̂_0)) lacks rigorous justification for the fine-tuning setting; no analysis of approximation error, convergence implications, or empirical comparison to alternatives like Monte Carlo estimation
Absence of theoretical guarantees: no convergence rates, sample complexity bounds, or characterization of how approximations and lazy updates affect policy optimality

Soft-optimal policies defined w.r.t. pre-trained p^pre rather than the current fine-tuned policy; while lazy updates apply, the theoretical implications and potential optimality loss from this design choice are not discussed

Hyperparameter sensitivity inadequately addressed: different α values required per domain (1.0 vs. 6.0), non-monotonic performance in K (Table 8), and limited principled guidance for selecting hyperparameters on new tasks

Conflicting metric signals on DNA task: VIDD better on Pred-Activity and ATAC-Acc but worse on 3-mer Corr (0.162 vs. 0.398 for DDPO) without explanation; raises questions about which aspects actually improve

Stability claims not rigorously validated: no explicit metrics (gradient variance, loss landscape smoothness, run-to-run variance); only convergence curves provided; comparison with DDPO conflates on-policy vs. off-policy paradigms

Limited scope: all experiments on discrete diffusion for biomolecules; applicability to continuous diffusion and other domains unclear; no analysis of failure modes or settings where VIDD underperforms

Implementation details unclear: how exactly is exp(v_t(x_t)/α) incorporated into the roll-in distribution in practice; what happens when x̂_0 predictions are poor; robustness to denoising errors not analyzed
Missing computational analysis: no wall-clock time comparisons, sample efficiency evaluation (reward evaluations needed), or detailed cost comparison with inference-time methods like Best-of-N

strengths: Addresses important problem: non-differentiable reward functions in biomolecular design are practically relevant and not handled well by existing gradient-based or PPO-style methods
Comprehensive experimental validation across three domains (protein, DNA, molecules) with multiple tasks, appropriate baselines, and extensive ablations demonstrating consistent improvements

Practical algorithmic design: posterior mean approximation for value functions is computationally efficient, lazy updates prevent target drift, mixed roll-in balances exploration-exploitation, and off-policy formulation enables flexible data collection
Consistent empirical improvements: VIDD achieves best or competitive performance across diverse tasks (protein SS-match 0.83 vs 0.81 DDPO, DNA Pred-Activity 8.28 vs 7.38 DDPO)
Clear theoretical motivation: Theorem 1 provides useful intuition about forward KL (VIDD) vs reverse KL (PPO) and mode-seeking behavior
Strong reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, task descriptions, and extensive supplementary results enable verification
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: core contribution (value-weighted MLE, Eq. 5) comes from Peters et al. 2010; soft-optimal policies (Eq. 2) are temperature-scaled pre-trained policies; main innovations are engineering choices (lazy updates, mixed roll-in) rather than fundamental algorithmic advances

Weak theoretical justification for critical approximations: posterior mean approximation v̂_t(x) ≈ r(x̂_0(x)) lacks justification; why it outperforms Monte Carlo (only M=4 tested) and trained value networks is unexplained; creates approximation error in exponential weighting

Value function definition-practice mismatch: soft-optimal policies (Eq. 3) define values as expectations under pre-trained trajectories, but p^out diverges from p^pre during training with only lazy updates; this discrepancy deserves thorough analysis and its effect on convergence is unclear

Significant hyperparameter sensitivity without principled guidance: multiple critical hyperparameters (α, K, β_s) are task-dependent; K=5 optimal for DNA but suboptimal for ss-match (Table 16); no principled framework for new domains limits practical adoption

Reward-diversity trade-off unresolved: Table 2 shows protein binding achieves 0.82 ipTM but diversity drops to 0.55 vs 0.90 pre-trained; Table 1 shows ss-match diversity 0.52 vs 0.91 pre-trained; no multi-objective optimization framework provided

Critical dependence on reward signal quality: Appendix G shows performance halves with 10% reward noise; in practice, reward models have biases and noise but method offers no robustness mechanisms; limits real-world deployment

Incremental improvements with incomplete statistical analysis: many improvements marginal relative to error bars; DNA 3-mer correlation shows VIDD worse (0.162 vs 0.398 DDPO); molecule task metrics show tied or worse performance on secondary objectives (Table 12)
Lack of theoretical analysis: no convergence guarantees, sample complexity analysis, or characterization of when approximations are valid; Theorem 1 connection is qualitative rather than quantitative

Limited scope and generalization: tested only on specific pre-trained models (EvoDiff, GDSS); no experiments varying architecture, model size, or training procedures; all domains biomolecular—generalization unclear

Incomplete experimental comparisons: DNA task comparison with DRAKES somewhat unfair (designed for differentiable rewards); molecule task shows VIDD underperforms on fragment/scaffold similarity suggesting mode coverage issues despite higher reward
